game.title: Jack's Letter Home
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 lines today
game.look: This letter is made up for the game, the way Jack writes letters home in Chapters 2 and 3. Every line has one misspelled word. Tap it, then tap the right spelling to ink the line clean. A clean letter gets a wax seal.

do: Read the line of the letter.

game.greet: Dear Aunt Arabella, Constance and Sarah,
game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for the next letter.

lines.text: At Coloma we walked right past the [famus] sawmill.
lines.why: fame drops its e before -ous: famous.
lines.miss: fame + ous: one letter of fame drops.

lines.text: At Shirt-tail Camp a crowd had [allready] decided Cut-Eye was guilty.
lines.why: already has one l: al + ready.
lines.miss: Find the word ready inside, with one l before it.

lines.text: Praiseworthy gave a speech so [persuasiv] that the crowd changed its mind.
lines.why: persuade: the d becomes s, then -ive. -ive always ends in e.
lines.miss: The ending -ive always ends with e.

lines.text: He won the [arguement] without a single law book.
lines.why: argue drops its e before -ment: argument.
lines.miss: argue + ment: one letter of argue drops.

lines.text: We dug and dug, and [finaly] we hit bedrock, and the dirt shone with gold!
lines.why: final + ly: keep both l's. finally.
lines.miss: final + ly: final ends in l, and -ly starts with l.

lines.text: My hands are so sore I can [barly] hold this pencil, but it is a good kind of sore.
lines.why: bare keeps its e before -ly: barely. Barley is a grain.
lines.miss: bare + ly: keep the whole word bare.

cards.title: A note before you read: words from 1963
cards.intro: This book was written in 1963. Two spots near the end of Chapter 17 talk about Chinese people in an old, unkind way. Here is what to know.

items.meaning: When the partners leave their claim, Chinese miners “with pigtails” move in to work it. Later the Mountain Ox eats oysters at the “Chinese chow chow” and orders a cook named Ah Lee around. Pigtails was a mocking word outsiders used for the long braids Chinese men wore.

Thousands of Chinese gold-seekers came to California in the early 1850s. Under China's rulers at the time, men had to wear their hair in one long braid called a queue, so cutting it off could keep a man from ever going home.

Chinese miners often worked old claims carefully and found gold others had missed, and many ran restaurants, laundries and stores. In 1852 California passed a $3-a-month tax on foreign miners that was aimed at them.

cards.note: Sources: PBS American Experience; Library of Congress.

virtue.name: hope

options.t: On the morning of the fight, Jack wonders if Praiseworthy has changed his mind. Praiseworthy says, “Not on your life, Jack. We'll make it.”
Before the fight, Praiseworthy says, “And anyway, I intend to lick him.”
After Praiseworthy dodges the first punches, Jack watches “with a leap of hope.”

art.title: Mountain Camp in California
art.alt: A watercolor of two white canvas tents joined together under tall pine trees, with a man walking past carrying a gun.
art.look: Joseph Goldsborough Bruff led a wagon company to California in 1849 and painted his camp in the Sierra Nevada that year: canvas tents under tall pines. In Chapter 17 the partners camp on their own claim on a hill above the river.
